title: Milinda's chariot, alone
hook: read the chariot dialogue whole (Milinda, Book 2)
tomorrow: what did the hare in the moon give away?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the jewel discourse: may all be safe, said on the strength of what's true. Today a king asks a monk his name, and gets an argument.
screen: `MAY ALL BE SAFE.` → `A KING ASKS A NAME.`

segments.voice: Every profile wants a bio. Who are you, in one line: artist, student, runner, overthinker. Pick one, and by Thursday it feels like a lie. In the Questions of King Milinda, a king meets a monk named Nagasena and asks his name. I'm called Nagasena, the monk says, but that's only a name. No person is found here. The king pounces. Then who is talking to me? Who keeps the precepts? Who meditates?
screen: `WHO ARE YOU, IN ONE LINE?` → `A KING MEETS A MONK.` → `"ONLY A NAME."`

segments.voice: Is your hair Nagasena, the king asks? Your nails, your skin, your feelings? No, each time. Then Nagasena is just a sound, and you've lied. Nagasena doesn't argue. He asks: how did you come here, your majesty? By chariot. Then show me the chariot. Is it the pole? The axle? The wheels, the frame, the reins? None of them. All the parts in a heap? No. Something apart from the parts? No. Then there's no chariot, and you've lied. The king, caught, gives the answer himself: chariot is the name we use when those parts come together. Exactly, says Nagasena. So is Nagasena. And he quotes a nun, Sister Vajira: as the word chariot is used for an assembly of parts, so we speak of a being when the parts of a person are there. This is the Buddhist teaching of anatta, not-self. It doesn't say you're nothing; the king did arrive in something. It says there's no fixed core hiding under the parts: body, feeling, perception, habits of mind, awareness, all changing together, with a name that's still useful. And that turns out to be freeing. A chariot of parts can be repaired.
screen: `IS YOUR HAIR NAGASENA?` · `SHOW ME THE CHARIOT.` · `A NAME FOR PARTS TOGETHER.` · `NOT NOTHING. NO FIXED CORE.` · then, large: `A CHARIOT OF PARTS.`

segments.voice: Pick up one object near you, a cup, a pen, your phone, and name its parts slowly, one per breath, until you can't find the cup among them. Set it down, still a cup. Then, more gently, do the same with the word I: a body, a feeling, a thought passing, the knowing of it, and let the name rest lightly on all of them.
Milinda's chariot: Nagasena's answer to a king. Chariot is a name for parts working together, and so is the name of a person.
Keep this one: a chariot of parts, and parts can always be repaired. Chariot parked.

screen: `DAY 1713 COUNTS.` → `THE PALI SOURCES, ALONE · 11 OF 12.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT DID THE HARE IN THE MOON GIVE AWAY?`

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use Nagasena's chariot to explain anatta, not-self, and meditators practice looking at body, feeling, perception, mental habits and awareness as changing parts rather than a fixed self.

fork.setup: your friend says, "i've always been a bad test-taker. it's just who i am." how would Nagasena's chariot answer?
options: "bad test-taker" names parts, like nerves and habits, and parts can change

fork.reveal: a name like chariot or bad test-taker is used for parts working together. there's no fixed core under them, and that's exactly why they can change.

original.note: Pali: not-self; no fixed core under the parts of a person.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhism says you don't really exist.
what it means: a person, like a chariot, is a name for parts working together, with no fixed core underneath.
what a scholar hears: Nagasena builds on a verse of the nun Vajira from the Samyutta Nikaya, and the book sets the talk in Sagala, with Milinda as a king of the Yonakas, the Greeks.
guess: a monk's proof that a self is a name for parts
the war chariot a Greek king gave to the Buddha
a parable about racing toward awakening quickly

chat.meaning: Nagasena showed that chariot is a name for parts working together; a person is the same, so there's no single core to find, and the name still works.

tie.story: Nagasena showed King Milinda that chariot names parts working together, and no single part is the chariot.

Nagasena.meaning: the monk who answers the king's questions

Vajira.meaning: a nun whose verse compares a person to a chariot

anatta.meaning: not-self: no fixed core under the parts of a person

notes: The chariot dialogue is paraphrased (Rhys Davids's 1890 translation is public domain, but the wording was not checked word for word, so nothing is quoted). Confirm the sequence: name, hair/nails/feelings, the chariot's parts, the king's own answer, the Vajira verse.
Vajira's verse (SN 5.10) is paraphrased; confirm that Nagasena cites it in the Milinda and that 'Sister Vajira' is fair.
The five aggregates are given in plain words (body, feeling, perception, habits of mind, awareness); confirm.
Trapdoor floor 3: the book places Milinda as king of the Yonakas ruling at Sagala; the common identification with the Greek king Menander is left out of the voice on purpose (claims rule). Confirm.
Mai storyline (1709–1722) day 5: the program asks for an artist's statement, 'who are you as an artist?'; Mai has six drafts and none feels like her.
Surprising fact: the king answers his own question; Nagasena only asks where the chariot is.
